questions.question: In George Orwell's '1984', what is the name of the totalitarian leader?
questions.explanation: Big Brother is the symbol of the Party's absolute power and constant surveillance over Oceania.
questions.funFact: Orwell originally titled the novel 'The Last Man in Europe' before his publisher suggested '1984'.

questions.question: In F. Scott Fitzgerald's 'The Great Gatsby', what does the green light symbolize?
options: Gatsby's hopes and dreams for the future
questions.explanation: The green light at the end of Daisy's dock represents Gatsby's unattainable dream of reuniting with her and recapturing the past.
questions.funFact: The Great Gatsby was actually considered a commercial failure during Fitzgerald's lifetime, selling fewer than 25,000 copies before he died.

questions.question: In William Shakespeare's 'Macbeth', what vision does Macbeth see before murdering King Duncan?
questions.explanation: Macbeth hallucinates a floating, blood-covered dagger pointing him toward Duncan's chamber.
questions.funFact: There is a long-standing theatrical superstition that saying 'Macbeth' inside a theater brings a curse; actors call it 'The Scottish Play' instead.

questions.question: Who is the author of 'The Catcher in the Rye'?
questions.explanation: J.D. Salinger wrote this iconic novel defining teenage alienation and angst, narrated by Holden Caulfield.
questions.funFact: After the massive success of the novel, Salinger became a recluse, stopping publication of his work and refusing almost all interviews for the rest of his life.

questions.question: In Arthur Miller's play 'The Crucible', the Salem witch trials are used as an allegory for what 20th-century event?
questions.explanation: Miller wrote the play to parallel the anti-communist 'witch hunts' led by Senator Joseph McCarthy in the 1950s.
questions.funFact: Because of this play, Arthur Miller was himself called before the House Un-American Activities Committee and convicted of contempt of Congress.

questions.question: What is the occupation of Guy Montag, the protagonist of Ray Bradbury's 'Fahrenheit 451'?
questions.explanation: In Bradbury's dystopian world, 'firemen' don't put out fires; they start them to burn illegal books.
questions.funFact: Bradbury wrote the novel in the basement of UCLA's library on a rented typewriter, paying 10 cents per half-hour.

questions.question: In Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein', what is the name of the monster?
questions.explanation: Victor Frankenstein never gives his creation a name; the creature is referred to as 'monster', 'fiend', or 'wretch'.
questions.funFact: Mary Shelley conceived the idea for the novel when she was just 18 years old during a ghost story competition with Lord Byron.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of dramatic irony?
options: The audience knows Juliet is just asleep, but Romeo thinks she's dead
A character says 'Great weather' during a hurricane
A postman is bitten by a dog
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows a critical piece of information that the characters do not.
questions.funFact: The term 'irony' comes from a character type in ancient Greek comedy called the 'eiron', the clever underdog who defeats a boastful opponent.

questions.question: In 'Lord of the Flies', what object is used to establish order and allow someone to speak during assemblies?
questions.explanation: The conch shell becomes a powerful symbol of civilization, rules, and democratic process among the stranded boys.
questions.funFact: William Golding once read the manuscript of the novel to his own boys as a bedtime story to see if they found it believable.

questions.question: What is the fatal flaw (hamartia) that leads to the downfall of a tragic hero often called?
questions.explanation: Hubris is excessive pride or self-confidence that brings about a character's ruin, a common theme in Greek tragedy.
questions.funFact: In ancient Athens, 'hubris' was actually a legal term for a crime involving the intentional use of violence to humiliate someone.

questions.question: In John Steinbeck's 'Of Mice and Men', what does Lennie desperately want to tend on the dream farm?
questions.explanation: Lennie, a large man with a mental disability, loves soft things and dreams of tending rabbits.
questions.funFact: Steinbeck's original title for the book was 'Something That Happened'. He changed it after reading a poem by Robert Burns.

questions.question: What classic novel opens with: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'?
questions.explanation: Charles Dickens' historical novel 'A Tale of Two Cities' begins with this famous paradoxical line.
questions.funFact: The 'two cities' referred to in the title are London and Paris during the time of the French Revolution.

questions.question: In 'To Kill a Mockingbird', what is Boo Radley's real first name?
questions.explanation: Boo's real name is Arthur Radley. He is a reclusive neighbor who eventually saves Scout and Jem.
questions.funFact: Harper Lee was childhood friends with Truman Capote, who inspired the character of Dill in the novel.

questions.question: What happens to the protagonist at the end of Kate Chopin's 'The Awakening'?
options: She drowns herself in the ocean
questions.explanation: Edna Pontellier swims far out into the Gulf of Mexico, unable to reconcile her desire for independence with the expectations of society.
questions.funFact: The novel was heavily censored upon its release in 1899 and effectively ended Kate Chopin's literary career due to public outrage.

questions.question: In Zora Neale Hurston's 'Their Eyes Were Watching God', what natural disaster forms the climax of the novel?
questions.explanation: The deadly 1928 Okeechobee hurricane forces Janie and Tea Cake to flee for their lives.
questions.funFact: Hurston wrote the novel in just seven weeks while doing anthropological research in Haiti.

questions.question: Which poet wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
questions.explanation: Dylan Thomas wrote this famous villanelle urging his dying father to fight against death.
questions.funFact: A 'villanelle' is a highly structured poem with 19 lines and a strict rhyme and repetition scheme.

questions.question: What is the name of the protagonist in Ralph Ellison's 'Invisible Man'?
questions.explanation: The narrator remains unnamed throughout the novel, emphasizing his metaphorical invisibility in a racist society.
questions.funFact: Ellison struggled for over 40 years to write a second novel but died before completing it; 'Invisible Man' was his only novel published during his lifetime.

questions.question: In Homer's 'The Odyssey', what is the name of the cyclops that Odysseus blinds?
questions.explanation: Odysseus tricks and blinds Polyphemus, angering the cyclops' father, Poseidon.
questions.funFact: To trick the cyclops, Odysseus tells him that his name is 'Nobody', so when the cyclops calls for help, he yells 'Nobody is hurting me!'

questions.question: Who wrote the classic American play 'A Streetcar Named Desire'?
questions.explanation: Tennessee Williams wrote the Pulitzer Prize-winning play featuring characters Blanche DuBois and Stanley Kowalski.
questions.funFact: The 'Streetcar Named Desire' was an actual trolley line in New Orleans that Williams could hear from his apartment.

questions.question: What is a 'bildungsroman'?
options: A novel dealing with one person's formative years or spiritual education
A poem written in blank verse
questions.explanation: A bildungsroman is a 'coming-of-age' story that tracks the moral and psychological growth of the main character.
questions.funFact: The term is German; 'Bildung' means education or shaping, and 'Roman' means novel.
